text: You now understand why GPUs are fast, and why their memory becomes the real constraint. This lesson grounds that in the actual products you'll provision: Azure's GPU VM families, and AWS's GPU instance families — and why picking the wrong one in each line is a real mistake, not just a suboptimal one.

Azure splits its GPU VMs into three lines that are genuinely not interchangeable. NC-series — NCv3 with V100s, or the newer NC A100 v4 — is the general-purpose GPU compute workhorse. ND-series, including ND A100 v4 and ND H100 v5, is purpose-built for large-scale training: NVLink connects GPUs within the VM, and InfiniBand connects VMs to each other, which is exactly what multi-node distributed training needs. NV-series, like NVadsA10 v5, targets visualization and virtual desktops — not training at all.

AWS draws the same line with different letters. P-series — P3 with V100s, P4d and P4de with A100s, and the newest P5 with H100s — is the training-focused line, adding NVLink and high-bandwidth EFA networking for distributed training. G-series — G4dn with T4s, G5 with A10Gs, and G6 with L4s — is the cost-effective line for inference serving, graphics, and smaller-scale fine-tuning. Same split as Azure, just different naming.

That interconnect is doing real work. Multi-node training has to constantly synchronize gradients across every GPU involved. NVLink speeds up GPU-to-GPU communication inside one server. InfiniBand and EFA speed up communication between separate servers. NV-series and G-series simply aren't built with that interconnect, because they were never meant to carry that job.

So before sizing anything, the question to ask isn't 'does this VM have a GPU attached.' It's whether that specific GPU model has enough VRAM for the job's working set, and enough interconnect bandwidth to other GPUs if it's a multi-node job. An eighty-gigabyte A100 and a sixteen-gigabyte T4 are both, technically, 'a GPU' — they are nowhere close to interchangeable.

With the real instance families in hand, the last piece is deciding when you even need one. Next lesson builds that framework: when a workload genuinely needs a GPU, and when a CPU is actually the smarter, cheaper choice.
